title: The bitter fruit made sweet
hook: tradition says a hungry Mardana ate bitter soapnuts at Nanak's word and found them sweet

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirtan, and your line, singing sets free. Did a tune reach someone, or reach you? Day seven hundred thirty-three.

Soapnuts. Some people still use them for laundry: small brown shells, dropped into a cloth bag, tossed in the wash, and they foam like soap. They aren't food. They're bitter enough to make a whole face fold up. Hold on to that, because in today's sakhi, a starving man is told to eat them. Yesterday Mardana was freed by a song. Today he's in the hills, hungry again, and the only food in sight grows on the wrong tree. Today: reetha.
screen: `SOAPNUTS: FOR LAUNDRY.` → `BITTER ENOUGH TO FOLD A FACE.` → `A HUNGRY MAN, THE WRONG TREE.`

segments.voice: In the tellings, Nanak and Mardana are walking through wild hill country, far from any village. Mardana is hungry, and says so, the way he does more than once in these stories. He's the very human one on the road, the one who gets tired and wants his dinner. Nanak points to a tree. It's a reetha, a soapnut tree. Eat, he says. Mardana hesitates. Soapnuts are bitter, and he knows it. But he trusts the Guru, picks one, and bites. And tradition says it was sweet. Sweet enough to fill him. Tradition links a gurdwara in those hills to this story, and it carries the tree's name. Now ask what the story knows. It knows something about hunger and about trust. Mardana doesn't get a feast. He gets the plain thing in front of him, the thing he'd have walked past. And it's the Guru's word that changes the taste. The Gurus' hymns speak of the Name as sweet. They speak of accepting what comes as the sweet will of God. So the sakhi turns that teaching into fruit. However the wonder is held, the scene makes a plain point: the same bite can taste bitter or sweet depending on what's brought to it. Met with complaint, it's soap. Received with thanks, in the Guru's name, it fed a hungry man. The sakhi doesn't ask Mardana to pretend the fruit isn't bitter. It asks him to take one bite.
screen: `HUNGRY IN THE HILLS.` · `EAT FROM THE SOAPNUT TREE.` · `TRUST, THEN A SWEET BITE.` · `THE SAME BITE, BITTER OR SWEET.` · then, large: `BITTER MADE SWEET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat something plain with thanks. If you have food nearby, take one plain thing: a piece of bread, a few grains of rice, a cracker, a glass of water. If not, simply remember the last plain thing you ate. Settle and breathe. Take it slowly. Notice the taste before you judge it. Then give thanks for it, out loud or inside, as if it were the best thing on the table. If you pray, you can say Waheguru before the first bite. The bell holds the time.
Reetha, the bitter soapnut Mardana ate at the Guru's word, hungry in the hills, and tradition says it was sweet.

Your line: bitter made sweet. Today, when you're handed something you didn't want, a task, a meal, a change of plan, take one bite of it with thanks before you complain. Day seven hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs tell the reetha sakhi as a story of trust and gratitude, and tradition links a gurdwara in the hills, named for the reetha tree, to it.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: the soapnut, the bitter fruit of today's sakhi.

trapdoor: what you thought: a magic trick with fruit.
what it means: a hungry man trusts the Guru's word, eats the plain bitter thing in front of him, and finds it sweet.
what a scholar hears: the sakhi turns the hymns' picture of the Name as sweet, and of accepting God's will as sweet, into something you can taste.
recall: the spoken telling in the gurdwara

notes: The reetha sakhi is associated with Gurdwara Reetha Sahib (Champawat district, Uttarakhand); some trace it to later tradition rather than the earliest janamsakhis. Confirm sourcing and whether 'a gurdwara in those hills' and the prashad detail are accurate.
Hymns on the Name as sweet ('mitha') and God's will as sweet ('tera kia meetha lage' is Guru Arjan, Asa, Ang 394): the script says 'the Gurus' hymns' for this reason; a Keeper may add Ang references.
Prashad detail (soapnuts given to pilgrims) cut from the voice pending confirmation.

Editor: cut sweeping 'nobody eats them' / 'everyone knows' and the uncited 'sweeter than anything the tongue can find'; the 'read it as a wonder / read it as a picture' pair, repeated from days 731–732, rephrased; hook no longer says 'your face'; fork answer moved off the middle slot.
Auditor: closing line 'the reetha story is gratitude, with a bitter edge' was vague, and 'it can feed you' read as a promise to the listener; both recast to stay inside the story.
